analysis.one_liner: Let Medicare negotiate drug prices directly, close the coverage gap, and allow cheaper drug imports from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed Medicare's drug benefit in three ways: it would have let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate prices directly with drug companies, just as the VA and Pentagon do; it would have eliminated the "donut hole," the gap where seniors pay full price for their drugs once costs pass a yearly limit; and it would have allowed Americans to import prescription drugs from Canada, with testing and anti-counterfeit packaging requirements. It never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, primarily seniors and people with disabilities, would have benefited. Government price negotiation and Canadian importation both aim to lower the prices they pay for prescription drugs, and eliminating the coverage gap would have ended the period each year when beneficiaries pay the full cost of their drugs out of pocket before catastrophic coverage begins.

how_it_helps.text: It repealed the 'non-interference' clause that forbids the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating with drug makers, and instead directed the Secretary to negotiate for the lowest possible prices, with the same authority the VA and Department of Defense use to buy drugs in bulk.
It eliminated the 'initial coverage limit' — the gap in Medicare drug coverage where beneficiaries pay full cost out of pocket before catastrophic coverage kicks in.
It allowed pharmacists, wholesalers, and individual consumers to import prescription drugs from Canada, with testing requirements and counterfeit-resistant packaging to protect against fake drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers would bear the cost through lower negotiated prices and competition from cheaper Canadian imports, and private Part D plans would lose their protected role as the negotiating intermediary. The federal government would also pick up the added cost of filling the coverage gap, since the bill included no funding offsets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private drug plans

drawbacks.text: Allowing drug importation from Canada raised safety and counterfeiting concerns, since drugs bought across borders are harder to track and verify; the bill tried to address this with testing rules and counterfeit-resistant packaging, but an importer who is not a wholesaler would not have been required to conduct the testing at all.

Eliminating the coverage gap (donut hole) in Medicare drug benefits would increase federal spending significantly, and the bill contained no taxes or offsets to pay for it, leaving the added cost unaddressed in the bill text.

Direct government price negotiation could have meant tighter formularies — a narrower list of covered drugs — for some beneficiaries, which is the tradeoff federal agencies like the VA make to get lower prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits were potentially large for the roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries: government negotiation and Canadian importation both aim at lower drug prices, and closing the coverage gap would have eliminated a real, annual financial hardship for seniors with high drug costs. The drawbacks are real: opening drug importation carries some counterfeit and safety risk, though the bill tried to manage it with testing and tamper-resistant packaging requirements; and eliminating the coverage gap raises federal spending with no funding mechanism in the bill text, which a supporter would have had to address. On balance the benefits to seniors outweigh the manageable costs, and the bill never faced a vote that would have tested that tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees in February 2007, and no committee ever acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2007 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee.
Within days it was sent to the health subcommittees of both committees — the last recorded actions before the bill died.
The bill ended with zero cosponsors, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
The 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009, and every bill not passed by then expires and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers, which kept the ban on Medicare price negotiation and on cheaper drug imports, and kept the coverage gap intact; Medicare beneficiaries kept paying full price for drugs in the gap.

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 27, 2007; it was his only recorded action on it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. John Dingell, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 27, 2007 and sent it to its Health Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Charles Rangel, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 27, 2007 and sent it to its Health Subcommittee; no further action was ever taken.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (PhRMA and member companies)
against.what_they_did: Opposed allowing Medicare price negotiation and drug importation and campaigned against such provisions during this period; no industry activity on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded support came from its single Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors of either party; the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split on the merits was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill took aim at three of the industry's legal protections: the ban on Medicare price negotiation, the ban on importing cheaper drugs from Canada, and (indirectly) the coverage gap that keeps seniors buying drugs at full price. None of it ever came to a vote, so the industry gave up nothing.

industries.industry: Prescription drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Under the Part D law in effect, private plans (not the government) negotiate with drug makers and manage formularies, and the 'non-interference' clause shields that arrangement. Giving the Secretary of HHS direct negotiating authority would have shifted that middleman role to the government.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug distribution and enforcement status quo (importation ban)
industries.note: The bill repealed the 2003 ban on reimportation and let individuals as well as pharmacists and wholesalers buy covered drugs from Canada, creating a legal channel for cheaper medicines that current law kept shut.

industries.industry: Packaging security and anti-counterfeiting technology vendors
industries.note: The bill required prescription drug packaging to carry counterfeit-resistant technology similar to the features on U.S. currency — optically variable inks, seals, and labels — creating a new mandated market for the vendors of those technologies.
